title: Salmonella Outbreak Linked to Mexican Jalapeños Expands to 32 States, CDC Reports

body_markdown:
A growing **Salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers imported from Mexico** has now affected 32 states across the United States, according to an update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Aug. 19, 2026.


Health officials say the outbreak has sickened at least **431 people** , including 86 newly reported cases. Fifty-seven people have been hospitalized, although no deaths have been reported so far. The investigation has focused on jalapeños originating from a farm in Sinaloa, Mexico, that were distributed in the United States earlier this year.


The expanding outbreak has prompted recalls involving fresh peppers and prepared foods containing the potentially contaminated ingredient. Consumers are being urged to check recalled products and avoid eating any items identified by health authorities.


## Salmonella Cases Reported Across 32 States


The number of states reporting infections has increased from 27 earlier this month to 32. The affected states are Alabama, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.


Some states have reported substantially more infections than others.


Colorado and Minnesota have each recorded more than 100 cases. Georgia and Illinois have each reported more than two dozen cases. Other affected states have reported between one and 14 infections.


Investigators say illnesses began as early as June 19 and continued through Aug. 2. Because foodborne illnesses can take time to be reported and investigated, health officials continue to monitor the situation for additional cases.


## Jalapeños and Recalled Food Products


The outbreak has been associated with jalapeños from a farm in Sinaloa, Mexico. The peppers were distributed in the United States earlier in 2026 and may have been used in a variety of prepared foods.


Several companies have issued recalls involving the peppers and products made with them. The companies named in the investigation include Taylor Fresh Foods, Whole Foods, NatureBest, and Hardie's Fresh Foods.


Retailers where affected peppers or products were sold include Kroger, Target, Trader Joe's, and Whole Foods Market.


Some recalled products include prepared dips. One example is **Spicy Jarlsberg Dip** , which was sold at Kroger. Another is **Taco Dip** , which was sold at Target.


Consumers should consult the latest recall information from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to determine whether products in their refrigerators or freezers are included in the recall. Because product details can change as investigations continue, checking official recall notices is particularly important.


Anyone who discovers a recalled product should not eat it. The product can generally be discarded or returned to the store where it was purchased for a refund, according to health authorities.


Restaurants, food-service businesses, and other establishments have also been advised not to sell or serve recalled jalapeños or foods containing them.


## What Are the Symptoms of Salmonella?


**Salmonella infection** , commonly known as salmonellosis, is a bacterial illness that can occur after consuming contaminated food or beverages.


Typical symptoms include:


- Diarrhea
- Fever
- Abdominal cramps
- Nausea
- Vomiting in some cases


Symptoms commonly begin within 12 to 72 hours after exposure, although the timing can vary.


Most people recover without serious complications, but Salmonella can become more severe in some individuals. Young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems can face a higher risk of complications.


The CDC advises people to contact a health care provider if they develop concerning symptoms. In particular, a fever above 102 degrees Fahrenheit accompanied by diarrhea is a reason to seek medical advice.


People experiencing severe or persistent symptoms should not attempt to diagnose or treat a potentially serious infection on their own.


## Mexican-Style Restaurants Investigated


One notable finding from the investigation involves restaurant dining.


Of 224 patients interviewed by investigators, approximately **91 percent said they had eaten at a Mexican-style restaurant before becoming ill** . The restaurants mentioned during the investigation included major chains such as Chipotle Mexican Grill and QDOBA.


This information does not mean that any particular restaurant chain is responsible for the outbreak. Instead, investigators are examining restaurant dining histories to identify common food exposures and determine how the Salmonella bacteria may have entered the food supply.


Fresh peppers can be used in salsa, sauces, dips, toppings, marinades, and other dishes, making them an important area of investigation when multiple people report eating similar foods.


## Food Safety Remains a Focus


The jalapeño investigation comes as U.S. health authorities are also responding to other foodborne illness concerns, including an increase in reported cases of cyclosporiasis.


Cyclosporiasis is caused by a parasite and is typically associated with consuming food or water contaminated with fecal matter. The simultaneous attention on multiple foodborne illnesses has increased public concern about food safety.


Acting Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Kyle Diamantas recently sought to reassure Americans about the nation's food supply, saying that the United States has a highly safe food system and that federal officials investigate numerous foodborne illness outbreaks each year.


The ongoing investigation illustrates why consumers should pay close attention to food recalls and follow instructions from public health agencies.


## What Consumers Should Do Now


People can take several practical steps to reduce their risk while the investigation continues.


First, check refrigerators, freezers, and kitchens for recalled jalapeños or prepared foods containing the affected peppers. Do not taste a product to determine whether it is safe.


Second, follow official recall instructions for disposal or returns. Wash hands and clean surfaces that may have come into contact with recalled food.


Consumers should also monitor updates from the CDC and FDA because additional products, retailers, or locations could potentially be identified as investigators learn more.


The current outbreak serves as a reminder that foodborne illnesses can spread across state lines through complex supply chains. A contaminated ingredient can potentially be incorporated into numerous products and distributed through multiple retailers and restaurants.


For now, health officials continue to investigate the source and scope of the Salmonella outbreak. With 431 reported cases across 32 states and 57 hospitalizations, consumers should remain alert to recall notices and avoid any recalled jalapeños or food products connected to the investigation.


**Source:** The Epoch Times.


**Disclaimer:** This article is for general informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Health information can change as investigations develop. For questions about Salmonella symptoms, exposure, treatment, or recalled food products, consult a qualified health professional and refer to current information from the CDC and FDA.
